pride_data.title: A Photocrosslinking Probe to Capture the Substrates of Caseinolytic Protease P
pride_data.projectDescription: Protein homeostasis in bacteria is regulated by proteases such as the tetradecameric caseinolytic protease P (ClpP). Although substrates of ClpP have been successfully deciphered in genetically engineered cells, methods which directly trap processed proteins within native cells remain elusive. Here, we introduce an in situ trapping strategy which utilizes trifunctional probes that bind to the active site serine of ClpP and capture adjacent substrates with an attached photocrosslinking moiety. After enrichment using an alkyne handle, substrate deconvolution by mass spectrometry (MS) is performed. We show that our two traps bind substoichiometrically to ClpP, retain protease activity, exhibit unprecedented selectivity for Staphylococcus aureus ClpP in living cells and capture numerous known and novel substrates. The exemplary validation of trapped hits using a targeted proteomics approach confirmed the fidelity of this technology. In conclusion, we provide a novel chemical platform suited for the discovery of serine protease substrates beyond genetic engineering.
pride_data.sampleProcessingProtocol: 990 µL bacteria suspension (OD600 = 40, in PBS-buffer) was incubated each with 10 µL trap1 or trap2 (final concentration: 10 µM) in the dark at 25 °C for 1 h with constant shaking at 450 rpm (Thermomixer comfort 5355, Eppendorf). Bacteria were centrifuged (6,000 g, 10 min, 4 °C) the supernatant was discarded, and cells were washed with 1 mL ice-cold PBS-buffer and centrifuged again (6,000 g, 10 min, 4 °C). Bacteria pellets were resuspended in 2 mL PBS-buffer and samples of one triplicate of each phenyl ester trap treated samples was transferred to wells of a 6-well plate and irradiated with UV-light (λ = 365 nm, Philips TL-D BLB, 18W) for 15 min under permanent cooling. Control samples were incubated for the same time in 2 mL Eppendorf tubes at 4 °C. Afterwards samples were centrifuged (6,000 g, 10 min, 4 °C) the supernatant was discarded, and bacteria were resuspended in 1 mL ice cold PBS-buffer. 5 µL lysostaphin solution (10 mg/mL in 20 mM sodium acetate buffer, pH = 4.5, recombinant lysostaphin from Staphylococcus simulans, L9043, Sigma Aldrich) was added and bacteria were incubated at 37 °C for 30 min with constant shaking at 1,400 rpm (Thermomixer comfort 5355, Eppendorf). Afterwards 20 µL 20% (v/v) SDS/PBS-buffer was added and the lysate was sonicated (10 s, 10% intensity, RT). Remaining cell debris was pelletized (10,000 g, 30 min, RT). Protein concentration was adjusted to 1 – 2 mg protein/mL by BCA-assay. Click chemistry was performed with 940 µL lysate and 60 µL Click master mix (10 µL Biotin-PEG-N3 10 mM (Jena Bioscience), 20 µL TCEP 52 mM, in H2O, 30 µL TBTA ligand (1.67 mM in 80% (v/v) t-BuOH, 20% (v/v) DMSO)). The reaction was started by addition of 10 µL CuSO4 (50 mM in ddH2O) and incubated in the dark at room temperature for 1 h. Afterwards proteins were precipitated by addition of 4 mL acetone ( 80 °C) and were incubated overnight at -20 °C. On the next day proteins were pelletized by centrifugation (21,000 g, 15 min, 4 °C), resuspended in 200 µL methanol (-80 °C, LC-MS grade, Fisher Scientific) by sonication (5 s, 10% intensity) and centrifuged again (21,000 g, 15 min, 4 °C). This step was repeated and afterwards proteins were solubilized in 500 µL 0.2% (w/v) SDS/PBS-buffer at room temperature by sonication and centrifuged again (10,000 g, 1 min, RT). Prior to enrichment 50 µL avidin-agarose bead suspension (Sigma Aldrich) per sample was washed three times with 1 mL 0.4% (w/v) SDS/PBS buffer (centrifugation 400 g, 2 min, RT). Solubilized proteins were incubated with avidin-agarose beads in LoBind Eppendorf tubes at room temperature for 1 h under continuous mixing. Afterwards beads were washed three times with 1 mL 0.2% (w/v) SDS/PBS-buffer (centrifugation: 400 g, 1 min, RT) and five times with 1 mL PBS-buffer (centrifugation: 400 g, 1 min, RT). Afterwards 25 µL digestion buffer I (2 M urea, 50 mM Tris-HCl, 5 ng/µL Trypsin (in 50 mM acetic acid, Promega), 1 mM DTT from 1 M stock in ddH2O, pH = 8.0) was added and samples were incubated for 30 min at 25 °C under constant shaking at 450 rpm (Thermomixer comfort 5355, Eppendorf). Then, 100 µL digestion buffer II (2 M urea, 50 mM Tris-HCl, 5 mM IAA, pH = 8.0) was added and samples were incubated overnight at 25 °C under constant shaking at 450 rpm (Thermomixer comfort 5355, Eppendorf). Remaining peptide solutions were desalted with SepPak® C18 columns. For LC-MS analysis peptide samples were dissolved in 25 µL 1% (v/v) aqueous FA, sonicated three times for 5 min and filtered with 0.22 µm Ultrafree-MC® centrifugal filters (Merck) which were equilibrated with 1% (v/v) aqueous FA. Filtrates were transferred to MS vials and analyzed by LC-MS/MS. Samples were analyzed with an UltiMate 3000 nano HPLC system (Dionex) using Acclaim C18 PepMap100 (75 μm ID x 2 cm) trap and Acclaim PepMap RSLC C18 (75 μm ID x 50 cm) separation columns in an EASY-spray setting coupled to an Orbitrap Fusion (Thermo Fisher Scientific Inc.). 1 μL peptide sample was loaded on the trap and washed with 0.1% (v/v) TFA, then transferred to the analytical column (buffer A: H2O with 0.1% (v/v) FA, buffer B: MeCN with 0.1% (v/v) FA, flow 0.4 μL/min, gradient: to 5% buffer B in 7 min, from 5% to 22% buffer B in 105 min, then to 32% buffer B in 10 min, to 90% buffer B in 10 min and hold at 90% buffer B for 10 min, then to 5% buffer B in 0.1 min and hold 5% buffer B for 9.9 min) and ionized by nanospray ionization. Orbitrap Fusion was operated in a TOP speed data dependent mode. Full scan acquisition was performed in the orbitrap at a resolution of R = 120,000 and an AGC target of 2.0e5 in a scan range of 300 – 1500 m/z with a maximum injection time of 50 ms. Peptide fragments were generated by higher-energy collisional dissociation with a collision energy of 30% and detected in the ion trap with scan rate set to ‘rapid’ and first mass set to 120 m/z.
pride_data.dataProcessingProtocol: Analysis of raw data was performed with MaxQuant software[12] (version 1.6.17.0) with settings on default. The following UniProtKB database was used for the search: S. aureus strain NCTC 8325/PS 47 (taxon identifier: 93061). Resulting data sets were further statistically analyzed with Perseus software[13] (version 1.6.2.3). For this, Protein groups files were loaded and LFQ intensities were selected as main columns. After log2 transformation, protein groups were filtered excluding those satisfying the criteria ‘potential contaminants’, ’reverse’ and ’only identified by sites’. Further filtering eliminated protein groups that featured only 50% or less valid values in the main columns. Missing values were replaced by imputation from a normal distribution (width: 0.3, down shift: 1.5, total matrix). After categorical annotation of LFQ intensities to groups +UV and –UV a two-sided student’s t test was applied with –UV as the single control group and Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate correction (FDR 0.05). Scatter plots were created by plotting student’s t-test difference (+UV vs. –UV, log2-scale) against student’s t-test p-value (log10-scale).
